title: HAWK-I image of NGC 1232
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1232 in near-infrared light, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
celestial: NGC 1232 · constellation Eridanus · about 65 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This is the spiral galaxy NGC 1232, seen in near-infrared light by HAWK-I on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The galaxy sits some 65 million light-years away in Eridanus, the River, and this picture ranks among the sharpest, most detailed views of it ever captured from the ground.

NGC 1232 is classed as an intermediate spiral, halfway between a spiral with a central bar and one without. Near-infrared light passes through dust more easily than visible light and highlights older stars, so a view like this reveals a different side of a galaxy.

There is a bit of history here. A visible-light image of NGC 1232 and its small companion, NGC 1232A, was among the first pictures the Very Large Telescope produced. HAWK-I, among the world's most powerful infrared imagers, returned to the same galaxy to show it in a new light.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.49 x 6.48 arcminutes) and distance (65 million light years), the frame spans roughly 123,000 × 123,000 light-years. Its light set out about 65 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image comes from the HAWK-I camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The Y filter is shown in blue, J in green, H in muddy brown and K in red.
